analysis.one_liner: Bans members of Congress and their spouses from owning or trading individual stocks.
analysis.headline: The bill to ban stock trading by members of Congress was referred to a Senate committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The PELOSI Act would bar sitting members of Congress and their spouses from owning or trading individual stocks, stock options, commodities, and similar investments during their time in office. Broad diversified funds and Treasury bonds would still be allowed, and members would have 180 days to sell off holdings or move them into a blind trust they cannot direct. Profits from banned trades would be turned over to the Treasury, violations could bring civil fines, and the Government Accountability Office would audit compliance every two years.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans, who currently sit on the other side of trades made by lawmakers who vote on the laws that move those very stocks. The ban removes the conflict of interest where a legislator can buy or sell shares of companies their committees regulate or their bills affect. It would also benefit everyday investors by reducing the risk that members profit on nonpublic information gathered on the job.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits members of Congress and their spouses from holding, buying, or selling individual securities, security futures, commodities, and synthetic equivalents during their term of service [S3].

Exempts only diversified mutual funds, diversified ETFs, Treasury securities, and a spouse's own workplace compensation, so the ban covers the assets through which insider-type trading actually happens [S3].
Requires any profit from a banned transaction to be disgorged to the Treasury and allows civil fines assessed by the ethics committees, with fines and their results published online [S3].
Requires annual written certifications of compliance published on a public website, plus a Government Accountability Office audit of member compliance within two years of enactment [S3].
Allows members 180 days to sell holdings to comply, and permits holdings in a qualified blind trust the member cannot direct, which addresses the objection that members cannot reasonably divest [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and their spouses, who would have to divest individual stocks and related investments or move them into blind trusts, giving up the ability to trade on information and timing available to them through their office. Financial advisers and brokerages that manage congressional trading accounts would also lose this line of business.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and their spouses

drawbacks.text: The bill lets each chamber's own ethics committee enforce the ban, and allows a member to appeal a fine to a floor vote in their own chamber, so the members subject to the rule remain in charge of policing it [S3].

Members with large, complicated holdings may face real costs and administrative burden in divesting or setting up blind trusts within 180 days, which the bill partly addresses through ethics-committee extensions for good-faith compliance efforts [S3].

A trading ban does not by itself stop members from steering policy toward assets they still hold through permitted diversified funds, or from profiting after leaving office through employment or board seats, which the bill does not address.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit — removing a direct conflict of interest between lawmakers' votes and their portfolios — is real and largely costless to the public. The costs fall almost entirely on the roughly 535 people covered by the ban, which is the point. The bill's design has a genuine weakness in letting congressional ethics committees, whose members themselves trade stocks, enforce the rule, and it does nothing about post-office influence peddling. Still, compared with the existing STOCK Act, which requires disclosure but allows trading, this is a substantially stronger rule, and its strongest fair objection is about enforcement, not purpose.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Josh Hawley introduced S. 439, the PELOSI Act, on February 15, 2023 [S1].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs the day it was introduced [S5].
No other member of the Senate cosponsored the bill — the cosponsor list shows zero additions over the life of the bill [S4].
The action history shows no activity after the committee referral: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action, through the end of the Congress [S5].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill expired without ever reaching the floor [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sitting members of Congress and their spouses came out ahead: they keep the ability to hold and trade individual stocks, including stocks of companies whose regulation they vote on, and face no new divestment requirement, fines, or compliance audits. No industry had to change its behavior either.

for.name: Sen. Josh Hawley
for.role: U.S. Senator from Missouri; sole sponsor of S. 439
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill banning congressional stock ownership and trading; no other senator joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
against.role: The committee of referral, chaired by a Democrat in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on February 15, 2023 and took no recorded action on it — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — for the remainder of the Congress [S5].

against.name: Senate Democratic leadership
against.role: Senate majority controlled floor scheduling in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for debate or a vote; no senator other than the sponsor signed on, and the bill died at the end of the Congress without floor action.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so there is no roll call to measure; the only on-the-record fact is that a single Republican sponsored the bill in a Democratic-controlled Senate and not one member of either party joined as a cosponsor [S4].

industries.industry: Members of Congress and their spouses
industries.note: The bill would force them to divest individual stocks, options, and commodities or move them into blind trusts, and would claw back any profits from banned trades. Their collective interest — keeping the ability to trade securities while writing the laws that move them — is directly contrary to the transparency the bill offers voters.

industries.industry: Securities brokerages and investment advisers serving congressional accounts
industries.note: A ban would eliminate a small but lucrative niche of individual-account trading by federal lawmakers. The effect on the broader financial industry is modest, since diversified funds and Treasury securities remain permitted.
